cc @clayjohn 

There might be a reason why clustered lighting works this way (especially when a custom `light()` function is involved), but I'm not sure.

> cc [@clayjohn](https://github.com/clayjohn)
> 
> There might be a reason why clustered lighting works this way (especially when a custom `light()` function is involved), but I'm not sure.

Yeah I had a feeling it had something to do with that, especially from the cluster grid appearance. If this is the intentional behaviour, then I suppose the solution is simply to always take attenuation into account in custom lighting functions.

I reported this because I thought it might reflect a possible invisible performance issue where objects that should be excluded from lighting calculations are not. Hopefully that's not the case here.

This looks like a clustering error to me. The light should not be processed unless it is in the same clusters that the pixel is in. 

What does the cluster debug view look like for this setup?

> This looks like a clustering error to me. The light should not be processed unless it is in the same clusters that the pixel is in.
> 
> What does the cluster debug view look like for this setup?

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/926b089e-2f87-4fa5-be18-65e062a6ed4d)

This is what the cluster view looks like when I'm orbiting a viewport with *NO* visible geometry in the scene, just one `OmniLight3D` that is 100 units away. Is this the expected result?

And on the off chance it rings any kind of a bell for someone:
I also experienced another Forward+ issue recently with non-directional lights where if I'm simply standing very close to one (such that everything around the camera is bathed in its light), I get huuuuge lag. I couldn't provide a minimal repro for that issue so I didn't submit a bug report, but it sounds suspiciously related to this.

@MajorMcDoom the way clustering works is to determine which fragments could potentially be effected by the light. It doesn't mean that a light MUST effect the fragment, that is up to the lighting logic to determine. It's a broad spectrum reduction so we hopefully end up only processing 1 or 2 lights per fragment, even if we add in a few false positives.

Take an omni light, this would be a circle around the center of the light with the radius of its falloff in screen space.
So yes, that recording in your last post is exactly what I would expect clustering to look like (the blockiness is because we're doing this check per tile to remain efficient).

It is still up to the lighting calculation to determine whether that fragment should be lit by this light. Normally the further away from the light you are, the less lit it would be (or if the light is behind the fragment, it should not be lit at all), but that is not the responsibility of the clustering logic, that is up to the lighting logic itself, and if your lighting logic says, fully light this fragment, it will happily do so for the entire tile.

This should be no different for compatibility nor mobile+, its just that how we determine if a light effects an object is different, but just because a light is evaluated for a given fragment, does not mean that light MUST be lighting that fragment. That is still up to the lighting logic to determine. You just only see the issues when a light is just on the edge, when it's almost near the point where it will be culled. In this case the light is evaluated for every fragment of that object, even if it only ends up lighting a few. In your use case I would expect the same sort of problems. 

That all said, the cluster logic does take the depth buffer into account. This is one of the reasons we do a depth prepass. For each tile the minimum and maximum depth value should be found, and if the circle of influence of the light does not overlap with this minimum and maximum depth, it should not be added to the cluster. So I wonder if there is an issue there. On your first recording in the OP, if the sphere of influence of the light does not touch the cube, I would expect the light not to be added to the cluster if it's obscured by the cube).

We still process lights that are behind the fragment, while in 99% of the cases those fragments will not be lit by this light, if translucence is applied, it still has an effect.

@BastiaanOlij If the light isn't in the same cluster as the pixel it shouldn't be processed. In this case the light is 100 units away from the cube and only has a radius of 5, so it definitely should not be processed
I can confirm the issue all the way back to 4.0.3. Likely the code for clustering has been broken all along.

> [@BastiaanOlij](https://github.com/BastiaanOlij) If the light isn't in the same cluster as the pixel it shouldn't be processed. In this case the light is 100 units away from the cube and only has a radius of 5, so it definitely should not be processed

Ah, do we ensure that the light falloff stays within the set range? I was under the false impression it could extend beyond seeing it's a logarithmic thing if I am not mistaken.
Yeah that sounds like we're not calculating the range of effect correctly during clustering.

@clayjohn @MajorMcDoom I went all the way back to Godot 4.0-stable and things work the same over all versions. As far as I can tell the system works as designed. There are two sides to this story. The first is whether the correct cluster tiles are hit: In the image above I changed the radius of the light to 10 because with a radius of 5 the gizmo icon was in the way :P But you can clearly see that with a radius of 10 the circle of the gizmo, which shows this radius, nicely goes through the tiles of the cluster. I've also confirmed this with the cluster debug draw. Just as a side note, the reason we clearly see the cluster tile shapes is because our light function outputs a fixed specular light value for any fragment that processes our light, so this is 100% expected behaviour. The second issue is the fact the light is so far behind. The cluster system is supposed to take depth into account. Now my assumption from my own experimentation with clustered lighting was that we would be reading from the depth buffer, first condensing it to a min and max value for depth. We do something similar for some of the other screen space effects. But this is not how things work. Instead all lights that hit a tile are written, but there are several depth layers to the cluster data into which we write the data. As best as I can tell from the code and from what I read in [2017_Sig_Improved_Culling_final.pdf](https://advances.realtimerendering.com/s2017/2017_Sig_Improved_Culling_final.pdf) we're segmenting into 32 depth slices. Our camera was set to a z-far of 4000, so each slice is 125 deep. ~~I'm not 100% sure here, it may be logarithmic as we've applying 1/z. It would have been really nice if this code had more documentation :)~~ Edit, this bit is me being dumb, it's a 1/z-far just to make this calculation easy. We're dividing depth into 32 equal slices. Anyway, our cube and our light are all still in this first slice and thus the light effects the cube. With the demo set to a z-far of 2900, the fragments on the cube are always in the first slice, while the light slowly moves from the first into the second slice. As we move our camera we can see how the light is evaluated: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bcb70001-e2ee-4ede-87ac-d747541b5033) So as far as I can tell, this is all working exactly as designed. The light is correctly filling the cluster data, and the correct fragments are picking up the light. Yes in this case we're getting a false positive but the approach here is likely much cheaper than condensing a z-buffer and reading from that. My only scratching my head moment here is that some of the other screen space effects already create a min/max condensed z-buffer so we're having that overhead anyway and we could thus use the result in our clustering if we wanted to. The bottom line though is, even with that improvement, the light function is responsible for doing the full check of whether the fragment is actually being effected by the light, there is no guarantee that just because a light is evaluated in the fragment shader, that it indeed fully lights that fragment. Note, @clayjohn , maybe the reason you through it was introduced in 4.0.3 is that I vaguely remember the default camera z-far value used to be much smaller than 4000, could be that in your testing it reverted to an older value?
